content: The water treatment system described operates with two filter units functioning in parallel. Disinfection is achieved through chlorination, and treated water is stored in four interconnected tanks located on-site at the water treatment facility. The distribution system supplies water to households through piped connections and public taps. At the household level, water is often stored in bulk, treated further (via filtration or boiling), and stored again after treatment. Key challenges affecting water quality include seasonal variations in source water quality, such as high turbidity during the wet season, and contamination from upstream runoff caused by human settlements, agricultural activities, and light industrial operations. Additionally, the system faces issues like intermittent water supply due to limited treatment plant capacity and unaccounted water losses from leakages and illegal connections. An operational monitoring plan (OMP) was developed to address these challenges. Sample points were strategically selected throughout the water supply system to monitor water quality. These points include locations at the start, middle, and end of the distribution system, with additional focus on vulnerable populations, such as schools and hospitals. In Bajo town, the largest population center in the Wangdue water supply system, four sample points were chosen. A monthly sampling schedule was established, ensuring that all 12 sample points are tested within a one-month period, with weekly sampling in Bajo town. The OMP outlines critical limits for water quality parameters, such as turbidity and chlorine levels, and specifies corrective actions if these limits are exceeded. Chlorine pumps and batch preparation are also checked to confirm proper operation. Additional water quality tests and flushing of water mains may be required if localized issues are identified. The glossary provides definitions of key terms related to water treatment and monitoring. For instance, chlorine disinfection refers to the use of chlorine to inactivate or kill microorganisms in drinking water, while turbidity describes the cloudiness of water caused by suspended particles. Residual chlorine is the remaining chlorine concentration in treated water that protects against recontamination during distribution. The World Health Organization (WHO), in partnership with AusAID (DFAT), has been promoting water safety plans (WSPs) in the South-East Asia region for over a decade. These plans aim to improve water quality and health outcomes by ensuring the sustainability of water supply systems. One major challenge in implementing WSPs, particularly in smaller systems, is maintaining effective operational monitoring. To address this, WHO engaged an expert to assist Bhutan and Timor-Leste in enhancing their monitoring practices through tailored training programs and the implementation of standard operating procedures (SOPs) for water quality monitoring. These SOPs, designed to be simple, clear, and comprehensive, are now published to meet the growing demand for training materials and technical guidance in this area.
